Moved a debate management motion to limit debate on the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (Abolition) Bill 2013 [No. 2] to conclude by noon, after the bill was earlier rejected by the Senate, saying the government wanted it passed by the House so it could return to the Senate within seven weeks.

Argued the government's alternative Direct Action policy would transfer $4 billion to $5 billion of taxpayer money to polluters every year without matching emissions targets, according to economists Ross Garnaut and Ken Henry, and said the Clean Energy Finance Corporation had already invested $590 million to leverage $1.8 billion in private investment, while renewable energy policy had grown household solar installations from about 7,400 to 1.1 million.

Supported the bill, saying abolishing the Clean Energy Finance Corporation would save more than $6 billion in borrowed money by 30 June 2017 and $350 million in interest costs, and accused Labor of hypocrisy for opposing the carbon tax repeal in the Senate while claiming publicly to oppose the tax.

Opposed the bill, saying the Clean Energy Finance Corporation had catalysed more than $1.55 billion in private investment from just $536 million committed, delivering a 3.9 million tonne reduction in carbon emissions, and cited University of New South Wales solar cell research the corporation could help commercialise.

Supported the bill, arguing it is unusual for government to operate banking-style investment services outside limited precedents like the Indigenous Land Corporation and Screen Australia, and said two-thirds of the corporation's claimed 3.88 million tonne emissions reduction came from the Taralga, Portland and Macarthur wind farms, which were already supported by the renewable energy target.

Opposed the bill, criticising the government for gagging debate on significant legislation despite its rhetoric about freedom, and argued the Senate committee's evidence and reasoning for rejecting the bill late last year deserved further consideration rather than a rushed vote.

This bill aims to improve how registered organisations like unions and employer groups are run and overseen.
It would set up a new independent body called the Registered Organisations Commission with stronger investigation powers.
Penalties would rise and new criminal offences would apply for serious misconduct by officers, mirroring rules for company directors.
Establishes the Registered Organisations Commission as an independent regulator.
Strengthens financial reporting and transparency rules by making some obligations enforceable as civil remedy provisions.
Increases civil penalties and creates criminal offences for serious breaches of officers' duties.
Expands disclosure requirements for officers' material personal interests and changes grounds for disqualification from office.
Gives the Commissioner investigation and information-gathering powers modelled on those in the Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act 2001.
Registered organisations, their branches, and their officers.
Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 - Second Reading - Agree with bill's main idea
Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 - Second Reading - Agree to the bill's main idea

Introduced a bill establishing a Registered Organisations Commission modelled on the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, citing Craig Thomson facing more than 150 fraud related charges and Michael Williamson pleading guilty to misusing almost $1 million of Health Services Union funds, and raising maximum penalties from 60 penalty units to 1,200 for individuals and 6,000 for a body corporate.

Opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013, arguing the government has not proven current regulation is failing after Labor tripled penalties last year, and cited employer group submissions warning the bill imposes obligations more onerous than the Corporations Act 2001 requires of company directors.

Supported the bill, arguing the Health Services Union scandal involving Craig Thomson and Michael Williamson showed existing regulation of registered organisations is inadequate, and welcomed the new Registered Organisations Commission's stronger investigation and disclosure powers to prevent similar misconduct.

Opposed the bill, arguing that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Act 2012 already strengthened regulation and that unions differ fundamentally from for-profit corporations, cited the Australian Industry Group's view that the disclosure rules are unfair to non-profit organisations, and called for the bill to be referred to the Senate references committee.

Supported the bill, arguing that the Health Services Union scandal, which involved nearly $1 million of members' funds, shows the need for the new Registered Organisations Commission with stronger, ASIC-style investigation powers, and noted that Bill Shorten's own bill had been given only five days of Senate committee scrutiny.

Supported the bill, arguing it will reassure workers that their union contributions cannot be misappropriated after the Thomson affair and the Health Services Union scandal, and noted that Fair Work Australia's registered organisations include employer bodies such as the Australian Education Union, not only trade unions.

Opposed the bill, said the Independent Education Union raised fees by two per cent to meet compliance costs under similar legislation already introduced by Campbell Newman in Queensland, and objected that executive members would have to register even their young children's Dollarmite bank accounts as personal interests.

Supported the bill, arguing that unions and employer bodies control large sums, illustrated by a leadership contest for the Queensland branch of the Transport Workers Union that oversaw about $11 million in assets, with $500,000 reportedly spent to change its leadership, showing the need for stronger financial oversight.

A motion to refer the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 to the Education and Employment References Committee was proposed on behalf of Senator Wong but was blocked by an objection.

The motion to refer the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 to the Education and Employment References Committee was moved, arguing that the bill was rushed with only one day of public hearings and that further scrutiny was needed, while opponents cited the government's election mandate and the need for higher penalties for union officials, referencing Justice North's criticism of existing penalties and the support of figures like Paul Howes.

Opposed the Fair Work Registered Organisations Amendment Bill, noted the unusual alignment of both the Australian Industry Group and unions in calling for more time to consider it, and accused the government of failing Holden workers and axing a fund meant to raise early childhood educators' wages.

Opposed the bill, tracing the coalition's industrial relations approach back to the Howard government's 2004 Senate takeover and Work Choices, said Labor's 2012 reforms had already tripled penalties for union misconduct following the Health Services Union scandal, and noted the National Workplace Relations Consultative Council itself had recommended the bill be delayed for further consultation.

Opposed the bill and called for Senate committee referral, noted Labor's 2012 reforms had already tripled penalties for registered organisation misconduct, cited the Australian Industry Group's submission that its 78 unpaid councillors would face disclosure requirements exceeding those on well-paid company directors, and said some proposed penalties would increase by two-thirds or more beyond existing law.

Opposed the bill, said the current Fair Work registered organisations framework, introduced in 2009 and strengthened in 2012, already imposes tough penalties, criticised new criminal penalties of up to $340,000 or five years imprisonment as unnecessary duplication of existing law, and noted a government member mentioned unions 25 times in one speech despite denying the bill targeted them.
The speaker tabled additional information from inquiries into amendments to the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 and the effectiveness of NAPLAN.

The speaker moved a motion to change committee memberships, discharging Senator Urquhart and appointing Senator Gallacher to the National Disability Insurance Scheme Joint Standing Committee, and appointing substitute members for several other committees including Wright, Milne, and Ludlam.

Closed debate on the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013, citing HSU and other union slush fund scandals to justify establishing an independent Registered Organisations Commission with stronger investigative powers and higher civil and criminal penalties aligned with the Corporations Act, and noted the Senate Standing Committee on Education and Employment's report tabled on 2 December.

Opposed the bill reviving the Australian Building and Construction Commission, said the 2001 Cole royal commission cost $66 million over 18 months without producing a single criminal conviction, criticised the bill for denying workers the right to silence and legal representation in secret interviews, and noted a former Federal Court judge had previously described the consulting firm's productivity modelling underpinning the bill as deeply flawed.

The ACCC would check whether savings from the repeal are passed on to consumers, especially in markets where competition is limited.
Introduce a new prohibition on price exploitation related to the carbon tax repeal for key goods like electricity and gas.
Give the ACCC monitoring powers to assess the effect of the repeal on prices.
Ban false or misleading representations about how the carbon tax repeal affects prices.
Businesses supplying key goods such as electricity and gas, and their customers.

This division relates to the Policies _[For a carbon price](/policies/3)_ and _[For renewable energy](/policies/20)_. The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2013-12-02.129.1) that: _At the end of the motion that the resumption of debate be made an order of debate for a later hour add: 'and the orders of the day for the resumption of the second reading debate on the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (Abolition) Bill 2013, and subsequently the Climate Change Authority (Abolition) Bill 2013, have precedence over this bill and the other related bills until determined.'_ (You can read the associated debate [here](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?id=2013-12-02.127.1). It commenced after 8:38 pm. ) Passing this motion means that the second reading debate about the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (Abolition) Bill 2013 and the Climate Change Authority (Abolition) Bill 2013 will be resumed before the debate about the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 and other related bills. The motion was introduced by Labor Senator [Penny Wong](http://publicwhip-rails.openaustraliafoundation.org.au/mp.php?mpn=Penny_Wong&mpc=Senate&house=senate). _Background to the bills_ The Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 was introduced into Parliament as part of a package of eleven bills to remove the [carbon pricing mechanism](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_pricing_in_Australia) and abolish the [Clean Energy Finance Corporation](http://www.cleanenergyfinancecorp.com.au/about-us.aspx) and the [Climate Change Authority](http://climatechangeauthority.gov.au/about). The eleven bills are: - [Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5137) - [True-up Shortfall Levy (General) (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5131)
Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 and related bills - Second Reading - Protect Australia from climate change

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2014-03-17.17.1) introduced by Labor Senator [Jacinta Collins](http://publicwhip-rails.openaustraliafoundation.org.au/mp.php?mpn=Jacinta_Collins&mpc=Senate&house=senate). The motion was for an amendment to be added to the end of the original motion, which was "_That these bills be now read a second time._" The words were: "_but the Senate calls on the Government to recognise the scientific expert consensus regarding [climate change](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change) and that the repeal of the carbon tax must be accompanied by the introduction of serious and comprehensive policies to address climate change._" Since the motion passed, these words will now be added to the original motion. Background to the bills The [Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5137) and related bills were introduced as a package to remove the [carbon pricing mechanism](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_pricing_in_Australia), which was introduced by the Australian Labor Party while in government. The Coalition described the mechanism as a “carbon tax” and removing it was a key policy platform during the 2013 election.(You can read more about the Coalition's policy to remove the carbon price [here](http://www.liberal.org.au/scrapping-carbon-tax-and-reducing-cost-living). ) The carbon pricing mechanism commenced on 1 July 2012.(For more information on the carbon pricing mechanism and how it works, please see the Clean Energy Regulator’s [website](http://www.cleanenergyregulator.gov.au/Carbon-Pricing-Mechanism/About-the-Mechanism/Pages/default.aspx).) It is an emissions trading scheme that puts a price on carbon emissions. It applies to “liable entities” (a group that includes companies that emit a high level of greenhouse gases). Moved the second reading of a bill imposing a true-up shortfall levy to recover overallocated assistance under the Jobs and Competitiveness Program, ensuring businesses are not over- or under-compensated in the 2013 to 2014 financial year.

Moved the second reading of a related bill imposing an excise-based true-up shortfall levy to recover the value of overallocated free carbon units issued under the Jobs and Competitiveness Program for the 2013 to 2014 financial year.

Moved a debate management motion to conclude debate on the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 and related bills by Thursday this week, arguing the election gave the coalition a mandate with 90 seats to Labor's 55, Labor's worst result since 1903.

Argued against the government's carbon tax repeal bills, saying the decade from 2001 to 2010 was the warmest on record, that Direct Action would cost households an estimated $1,200 a year without a legislated cap on emissions, and noted that under Labor wind power generation trebled and 24,000 renewable energy jobs were created.

Continued opposing the carbon tax repeal bills, saying NASA had confirmed 97 per cent of actively publishing climate scientists agree human activity causes global warming, cited the IPCC's Fifth Assessment Report finding 95 per cent certainty on human-caused climate change, and noted global average surface temperatures had risen by almost 0.9 degrees Celsius since 1880.

Supported repealing the carbon tax, saying Sydney households had faced a 57 per cent increase in power bills since 2010, and noted Australia's $25 a tonne carbon price was the highest in the world with no other country imposing an economy-wide carbon tax.

Supported repealing the carbon tax, citing a 15.3 per cent rise in electricity prices in the first quarter after its introduction and an almost 11 per cent swing to the Liberal Party in his Bass electorate at the 2013 election, and said the tax cost the economy $9 billion.

Opposed repealing the carbon tax, citing a $4.4 million grant that cut the JBS meatworks' carbon price liability by $790,000 a year in his Ipswich electorate, and said the coalition's review had put a $1.2 million LED street lighting grant for Ipswich in jeopardy.

Argued that the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 would fulfil the coalition's promise to repeal the carbon tax, restore trust and reduce costs, while claiming the tax disadvantaged Australian businesses, consumers and jobs and had negligible effects on global temperatures.

Argued that emissions trading would burden Australia's coal and aluminium industries, questioned who would benefit from it, and advocated ethanol as a way to reduce transport emissions, citing international use and potential reductions from grain and sugarcane ethanol.

Supported repealing the Clean Energy Act 2011 and associated charges acts, abolishing related assistance and institutions, and using the ACCC to ensure prices fell, arguing the carbon tax harmed households, businesses and jobs and that the election endorsed repeal.

Argued for repealing the carbon tax, citing Alcoa's warning that the tax would cost Australian aluminium producers at least $60 a tonne while its Western Australian refineries had already cut emissions per tonne by more than 20 per cent since 1990 without one, and noted Western Power's own trigger point for changing behaviour was $90 a tonne.
Argued for repealing the carbon tax, citing about 13,000 small businesses in Calare and an example of a $10,000 annual electricity bill rising by $1,000 a year because of the tax.

Opposed repealing the carbon tax, arguing the science of climate change is settled and defending the scheme's three-year fixed price period, and noted Australia's carbon price has worked since 1 July 2012, comparing it to California's emissions trading scheme covering about 60 per cent of its economy since 1 January 2013 and China's new carbon pricing trials in seven provinces.

Supported repealing the carbon tax, citing government modelling that the carbon price was set to reach $56 a tonne, said scrapping it would leave average households $550 a year better off from 2014 to 2015, and cited an Australian Industry Group survey of 485 businesses that found manufacturing energy costs rose by an average of 14.5 per cent because of the tax.

Argued that most electricity price rises in New South Wales stemmed from state network costs rather than the carbon price, said Direct Action modelling showed it would cost Australian households $1,200, and quoted Malcolm Turnbull's December 2009 criticism of the then Opposition Leader's shifting positions on emissions trading, alongside 97 per cent scientific agreement on climate change.

Recalled then Prime Minister Gillard's 2010 promise of no carbon tax before it was legislated on 11 October 2012, cited local business examples in the Higgins electorate of sharp bill increases attributed to a 'carbon charge', and said Treasury modelling showed repeal would save households around $550 a year.

Supported the bill to reduce Territory bills and argued that the carbon tax should be repealed, saying it increased costs for households, businesses and local government without delivering environmental benefits. Cited Treasury modelling of an average household cost reduction of around $550 during the 2014-15 financial year and urged Territory representatives to support repeal.

Opposed the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013, citing a 6.1 per cent drop in electricity sector emissions equivalent to 12 million tonnes of carbon dioxide, a 30 per cent surge in renewable energy generation, and more than 150,000 jobs created since the carbon price began.

Supported repealing the carbon tax, arguing it had raised $16 billion over two years without reducing domestic emissions, promised families would be $550 a year better off once it is scrapped, and confirmed the government retains the same five per cent emissions reduction target by 2020 that Labor had set.

Opposed repealing the carbon tax, noting that sixty-odd thousand Australians attended climate change rallies around the country on the weekend, including firefighters concerned about the impact on their work, and argued the government's course of cutting the Clean Energy Finance Corporation and scientists' funding is the wrong direction.

Raised a point of order accusing the Prime Minister of misleading the House by referring to the 2009 stimulus bill when the Leader of the Opposition had asked about the Commonwealth Inscribed Stock Amendment Bill, and sought leave to table Hansard to correct the record.

Moved to suspend standing orders so the Commonwealth Inscribed Stock Amendment Bill 2013 could proceed through all stages on 13 November 2013, with a managed debate and consideration in detail limited to 60 minutes. Argued that prompt passage was needed to address the debt ceiling and maintain confidence in markets and the economy.

Argued the coalition inherited no debt and $50 billion in savings on leaving office, while Labor progressively raised the debt limit to $300 billion, and said servicing Labor's debt now costs $10 billion a year in interest, describing the increase as an unfortunate but necessary clean-up.

Argued that the coalition left no debt or debt ceiling in 2007, and criticised Labor for repeatedly raising the ceiling from $75 billion to $300 billion while now opposing the government's request for a further increase.

The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to allow the Commonwealth Inscribed Stock Amendment Bill 2013 to be considered during the current sittings, with royal assent required by the end of November 2013 to increase the legislative limit on Commonwealth Government Securities.
The speaker moved to waive standing order requirements for the Commonwealth Inscribed Stock Amendment Bill 2013 so it could be considered in the current sittings; the motion was agreed to.

The speaker moved to schedule the Australian Capital Territory Water Management Legislation Amendment Bill 2013 for 12:45 pm and the Commonwealth Inscribed Stock Amendment Bill 2013 for debate until 2 pm, arguing the opposition supports the stock bill but needs more time for substantive discussion on debt ceiling changes, and criticised poor time management in the chamber.

Congratulated the member for Moore on his maiden speech, and moved to suspend standing orders so the House could immediately consider the Senate's requested and further amendments to the Commonwealth Inscribed Stock Amendment Bill 2013.

Defended the Commonwealth Inscribed Stock Amendment Bill 2013, arguing Labor turned $45 billion of net assets into more than $400 billion of debt, and noted Labor promised a budget surplus on over 600 occasions before delivering a deficit of nearly $31 billion.

Opposed the bill, accusing the coalition of hypocrisy for lecturing Labor on obstruction after itself blocking savings measures like indexing the private health insurance rebate and opposing the Malaysia people transfer agreement in the previous parliament.
The House of Representatives agreed to the Senate's further amendments to the Commonwealth Inscribed Stock Amendment Bill 2013 and made the amendments requested by the Senate.
